extracted.intended_audience: aspiring professional pianists, advanced piano students, and piano teachers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for daily technical practice, memorization, rhythmic development, and tonal coloring for pianists preparing repertoire and performance-level playing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Daily time devotion
rubrics_metrics.description: Most of the artists give a large portion of each day to the work; a professional pianist must give a number of hours each day to actual practise at the keyboard, besides what is done away from it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several cited pianists give multiple hours daily (e.g., Germaine Schnitzer six hours, Burnham entire mornings); mental work continues even when not at the instrument. Plan and protect long, regular studio hours.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate technical practice (technic apart from pieces)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many great pianists believe in daily technic practise, or the study of pure technic apart from pieces; scales, chords, arpeggios and octaves constitute their daily bread.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve dedicated time to technic (e.g., Bachaus: practises technic about an hour a day including Bach; Burnham: at least one hour to technic). Treat technique like 'mechanical upkeep'—regular tinkering and overhauls once or twice a week.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scales and arpeggios
rubrics_metrics.description: Scales and arpeggios are of great importance; practise them in various touches, oftener in legato since it is more difficult and beautiful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select a few keys at a time rather than cycling all keys each session; vary touch, velocity, and dynamics; some artists practice scales in a single key for long stretches (Paderewski).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Bach in technique
rubrics_metrics.description: All artists use Bach in connection with their technic practise; the works of Bach embody pure technic principles and are considered a daily necessity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include Bach (inventions, preludes & fugues) as core technical material; some teachers assign learning sets in every key and transposition exercises using Bach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus and selectivity in etude practice
rubrics_metrics.description: It is better to perfect a few etudes than to play at so many.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perfecting one selection (e.g., an etude) thoroughly, transposing it and polishing it fully, is more effective than superficial practice of many.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventing technical exercises from repertoire
rubrics_metrics.description: Artists invent exercises out of the pieces: play both-hand passages with one hand, turn single notes into octaves, use more difficult fingering, change rhythm, etc., to increase the effort required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use customized, passage-specific exercises to strengthen weaker fingers and make original passages seem easy by comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transposition as technical training
rubrics_metrics.description: Transposition is a means to acquire technical mastery; artists practice pieces through different keys to deepen technical and musical command.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transposing entire sets (e.g., Bach inventions or all preludes and fugues) into every key was cited as an effective, even extreme, method for mastering technic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Slow, clarity-first practice (avoid training for speed)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many pianists practise very slowly, preferring clarity and good tone; if a passage is mastered slowly with clearness, velocity will follow when needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin slowly, attend to clearness, tone, fingering, accents and dynamics; only employ velocity after the piece is thoroughly learned. Avoid practising fast in ways that sacrifice clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Velocity develops from comprehension
rubrics_metrics.description: Some masters believe velocity is inherent or develops after full comprehension; one should not 'work for velocity' prematurely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concentrate on understanding and mastery; speed will come without forced fast repetitions if the passage is well learned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technic overhaul and maintenance
rubrics_metrics.description: Technic must be kept in running order by constantly tinkering and periodically overhauling to ensure everything is in order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schedule periodic review/overhaul sessions (once or twice a week suggested) to check and correct technical habits; treat technique like machinery needing maintenance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice variety of touches and tonal gradations
rubrics_metrics.description: Practice scales, chords, arpeggios and other technical forms with every possible variety of touch and tone to secure tonal variety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experiment with touches, dynamics, velocity and shading to create contrasts of light and shade; tonal gradations are essential to expressive playing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use metronome judiciously
rubrics_metrics.description: Correct use (not abuse) of the metronome is of great assistance in establishing firm rhythmic sense; if pupils have poor sense of rhythm, there is no remedy equal to practising with the metronome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ the metronome daily until rhythmic results are evident, then ease the discipline; recognize that delicate rhythmic nuances (e.g., Chopin mazurka) also require innate rhythmic gifts beyond mechanical practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop a well-trained rhythmic sense
rubrics_metrics.description: Rhythm is one of the pianist's most important assets; a perfect time sense separates artist from amateur and must be cultivated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work on counting, grouping notes correctly, and internalizing time so that rhythm is reliable even under interpretive fluctuations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone color and fingering choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Tone color depends in part on the fingering used; certain fingers produce different qualities (e.g., third finger 'warm', fifth finger 'cold').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose fingerings intentionally to achieve desired tonal color; study singers and painters for ideas of tonal shading and color analogy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strive for tonal variety and expressive contrast
rubrics_metrics.description: The pianist must continually strive for variety of tone and tonal coloring—contrast of light and shade, tonal gradations, and subtleties of nuance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use differences of touch, shading and dynamic contrast; some seemingly harsh tones may be beautiful in context; study great players (Paderewski, Hofmann) as models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study color effects from other arts and nature
rubrics_metrics.description: The pianist can study color effects in theatre, opera, painting and nature and translate those perceptions into tonal color in playing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe theatrical lighting, stage action, and singers to expand one's palette of tonal associations and expressive possibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memorize away from the instrument
rubrics_metrics.description: Leschetizky advises memorizing away from the instrument to avoid useless repetition; learn short passages separately with each hand, then try them on the piano.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid senseless repetition at the keyboard; analyze and fix passages mentally before returning to the instrument for verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memorize phrase by phrase after analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Memorizing must be done phrase by phrase after the composition has been thoroughly analyzed as to keys, chords, and construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commit ideas in small units (two or four measures) and proceed systematically; hands-alone practice for very intricate passages may be used selectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thorough analysis for secure memorization
rubrics_metrics.description: To master a passage by heart, analyze it thoroughly—know the notes, sequences, positions on the keyboard, fingering and hand positions so fingers 'know where to go'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deep analytical work ('know just what the notes are') reduces the need for mindless repetition and produces stable memorization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematic and regular memorization builds repertoire
rubrics_metrics.description: A disciplined memorizing habit allows a player who studies five or six hours daily to commit about one page per day—leading to a large, performance-ready repertoire (Leschetizky suggested ~200 pieces in repertoire).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work a little each day, systematically, to build repertoire progressively; even halving the optimistic estimate yields substantial yearly gains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep repertoire in repair through scheduled review
rubrics_metrics.description: A repertoire once committed must be constantly kept in repair; public players generally have a regular system of repetition so compositions are gone over at least once a week.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize weekly rotation (e.g., start with classics, end with modern works); not merely play through pieces but overhaul weak spots with slow, careful practice using printed pages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personalize methods and routines
rubrics_metrics.description: Each player must find the path to memorizing and technical mastery best suited to his temperament; masters agree analysis and concentration are prime factors, but methods may vary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Try different approaches until discovering the most efficient and thorough method; remain open to adapting techniques to individual needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concentration, perseverance, and devotion distinguish artists
rubrics_metrics.description: The difference between artist and talented amateur often lies in absolute concentration, perseverance and devotion to the highest ideals; even greatest artists must toil over technic and memorize bit by bit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain high standards of focus and persistence; treat practice as disciplined, purposeful work rather than casual repetition.
